stem:
An emergency registrar assesses a 17-year-old with sudden severe right-sided pelvic pain and vomiting. The pain briefly settled, then returned. Pregnancy testing is negative and she is afebrile. Ultrasound shows an enlarged right ovary with stromal oedema and a 5-cm cyst; arterial and venous flow are still detected. She remains tender despite analgesia.

Which next step is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Admit for analgesia and repeat Doppler in six hours, operating if flow is lost
options.explanation: Arterial and venous flow can persist in torsion because of the ovary’s dual supply; waiting for flow to disappear risks losing the ovary.

options.label: B
options.text: Arrange CT abdomen to exclude appendicitis before gynaecological referral
options.explanation: The ultrasound already shows an enlarged oedematous ovary with a cyst, which explains the picture; CT adds radiation and delay without changing the need for surgery.

options.label: C
options.text: Book elective laparoscopic cystectomy once the pain has settled
options.explanation: Intermittent severe pain with vomiting and an oedematous ovary suggests active torsion now; deferring surgery until pain settles risks infarction.

options.label: D
options.text: Arrange urgent gynaecological assessment for diagnostic laparoscopy
options.explanation: Torsion is a clinical and surgical diagnosis; a suggestive presentation with an enlarged oedematous ovary warrants urgent laparoscopy to detort and preserve the ovary.

options.label: E
options.text: Arrange pelvic MRI to confirm torsion before any surgical decision
options.explanation: MRI delays treatment and a normal-looking result would not exclude intermittent torsion; the decision is made on clinical grounds.

context: Preserved Doppler flow does not exclude ovarian torsion; a convincing clinical presentation requires urgent surgical assessment.
